---
title: Super-Sample Covariance
---

This page describes the super-sample covariance (SSC) matrix $S_{ij}$ computed by
[[numcosmo|NcXcorSSCSij]], and how it enters the Gaussian cluster number-count
likelihood [[numcosmo|NcDataClusterNCountsGauss]].

## The effect

A survey measures a finite volume, so density modes with wavelengths longer than
the footprint are not observable. They shift the mean density inside the volume
away from the cosmic mean, and every count in that volume changes with that shift. Writing $\delta_{\mathrm{b},i}$ for the mean
matter density contrast over redshift bin $i$, the expected counts respond
linearly through the halo bias $b_i$,
$$
N_i = \bar{N}_i \left(1 + b_i\,\delta_{\mathrm{b},i}\right),
$$
and since $\delta_{\mathrm{b},i}$ is itself a random variable the counts have a
covariance in addition to the Poisson one,
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(N_i, N_j) = \bar{N}_i\,\delta_{ij} + b_i b_j\,S_{ij},
\qquad
S_{ij} \equiv \left\langle \delta_{\mathrm{b},i}\,\delta_{\mathrm{b},j} \right\rangle .
$$
The first term is the shot noise; the second is the super-sample term. Because
every bin contains the same long-wavelength modes, $S_{ij}$ is not diagonal: it
correlates bins that do not overlap in redshift at all. See
@TakadaHu2013 and @LacasaGrain2019 for the derivation of the effect
and of the estimator used here.

## $S_{ij}$ as an angular power spectrum

The bin-averaged contrast $\delta_{\mathrm{b},i}$ is the matter contrast smoothed
by the survey window: a top hat in the radial direction over bin $i$, and the
survey footprint on the sky. Separating the two, $S_{ij}$ becomes a sum over
multipoles of the angular power spectrum $C^{ij}_\ell$ of the radially averaged
contrast.

Define the radial window of bin $i$ to be a top hat normalized to unit integral
in comoving volume, so that $\delta_{\mathrm{b},i}$ is a plain volume average and
not a weighted one. Then, for a full-sky survey, only the monopole contributes,
$$
S_{ij} = \frac{C^{ij}_0}{4\pi} .
$$
For a real footprint, described by a mask $W(\hat{n})$ with angular power
spectrum $C^{\mathrm{mask}}_\ell$ and sky fraction
$f_{\mathrm{sky}} = \sqrt{C^{\mathrm{mask}}_0 / 4\pi}$, the mask couples
multipoles and the estimator becomes
$$
S_{ij} = \frac{1}{\left(4\pi f_{\mathrm{sky}}\right)^2}
  \sum_{\ell=0}^{\ell_{\max}} (2\ell+1)\,C^{\mathrm{mask}}_\ell\,C^{ij}_\ell .
$$
Substituting $f_{\mathrm{sky}}^2 = C^{\mathrm{mask}}_0 / 4\pi$ removes the square
root and gives the form actually evaluated,
$$
S_{ij} = \frac{1}{4\pi\,C^{\mathrm{mask}}_0}
  \sum_{\ell=0}^{\ell_{\max}} (2\ell+1)\,C^{\mathrm{mask}}_\ell\,C^{ij}_\ell .
$$
The full-sky case is the value $C^{\mathrm{mask}}_\ell = 4\pi\,\delta_{\ell 0}$ in this
expression, for which the sum reduces to $C^{ij}_0 / 4\pi$. [[numcosmo|NcXcorSSCSij]]
uses that spectrum as its default footprint, so the full-sky and the masked cases run
the same code.

### Finite area

A survey described only by its area uses the full-sky matrix rescaled by the sky
fraction,
$$
S_{ij} = \frac{S^{\rm fullsky}_{ij}}{f_{\rm sky}},
\qquad f_{\rm sky} = \frac{\Omega}{4\pi} .
$$
This correction uses the solid angle of the footprint and not its shape. It
includes the dominant effect of a finite footprint: a smaller volume contains fewer
long-wavelength modes, so the mean density in it has a larger variance. Like the
full-sky case, it needs only the monopole. `nc_xcor_ssc_sij_set_area()` selects it.

The full-sky $S_{ij}$ underestimates the super-sample variance of a survey with
$f_{\rm sky} < 1$: the rescaling multiplies $S_{ij}$ by $1/f_{\rm sky} > 1$, so without
it the parameter constraints are too tight. The factor is about $2.3$ for
$18\,000\ \mathrm{deg}^2$ and about $14$ for $3\,000\ \mathrm{deg}^2$. A survey that
does not cover the full sky needs either an area or a mask.

The truncation $\ell_{\max}$ is set by the fraction of the mask variance
$\sum_\ell (2\ell+1) C^{\mathrm{mask}}_\ell / 4\pi$ to recover; `find_lmax` in
`numcosmo_py.ssc` returns the smallest $\ell_{\max}$ that meets a requested tolerance.

## Non-Limber at every multipole

The Limber approximation replaces the spherical Bessel functions in the radial
integral by a delta function, and is accurate only when the window is broad compared
with the oscillation scale, that is, at high $\ell$. The sum for $S_{ij}$ is dominated
by the lowest multipoles, $\ell = 0$ for a full-sky survey, where the approximation does
not apply. It also gives zero for the cross spectrum of two bins with disjoint redshift
support, while the true $C^{ij}_\ell$ is nonzero: two disjoint shells are windows on the
same three-dimensional field, and the non-Limber calculation couples them through the
outer $k$ integral.

[[numcosmo|NcXcorSSCSij]] therefore sets `l_limber = -1` on every kernel, and the
radial integrals are computed by
[UltraLevin](../../ncm/specfunc/sbessel_projection.qmd) through
[[numcosmo|NcXcorSolver]].

## Numerical accuracy

$S_{ij}$ is a sum of angular power spectra, so its accuracy is that of the
$C^{ij}_\ell$. [Accuracy Control for Angular Power
Spectra](../../../tutorials/python/xcor_accuracy.qmd) measures it on cluster top-hat bins
at the defaults of [[numcosmo|NcXcorSSCSij]], `NcXcorKernel:reltol` $10^{-6}$ and
`NcXcorKernel:peak-epsilon` $10^{-5}$. The error of a cross spectrum is measured
against $\sqrt{C^{ii}_\ell C^{jj}_\ell}$: at these defaults the cross spectrum of two
separated bins deviates from a tighter closure, and the certified separated pair X14
from its certified value, by less than peak-epsilon of that scale, see the tutorial's
[certified values](../../../tutorials/python/xcor_accuracy.qmd#sec-certified). A cross spectrum of separated
bins is three orders of magnitude below that scale, so its relative error is larger by
the same factor. The off-diagonal $S_{ij}$ of separated bins are in the same case: for
seven top-hat bins over $z \in [0.1, 0.8]$, $|S_{06}|$ is four orders of magnitude below
$S_{00}$.

[[numcosmo|NcXcorSSCSij]] rebuilds $S_{ij}$ at every likelihood step, so its defaults are
looser than the validation setting of the tutorial; on its cluster top-hat, peak-epsilon
$10^{-6}$ costs 1.5 times the closure nodes of $10^{-5}$, see the tutorial's
[closure cost](../../../tutorials/python/xcor_accuracy.qmd#sec-tolerances). Below $10^{-6}$
`nc_xcor_kernel_set_peak_epsilon` warns. The quadrature is
`NC_XCOR_METHOD_KERNEL_EXACT`, which integrates the closures exactly on the common
refinement of their panels and has no tolerance.

## Varying $S_{ij}$ along a chain

$S_{ij}$ depends on cosmology, like every other part of the covariance. A
reference analysis may still hold it at a fiducial value and vary only the mean
and the Poisson term, which is much cheaper: recomputing $S_{ij}$ per likelihood
step costs about $+60\%$ over the rest of the evaluation for a full-sky or
area-rescaled footprint, and roughly a factor of six for a masked one, where
every multipole up to $\ell_{\max}$ must be solved.

Setting [[numcosmo|NcDataClusterNCountsGauss]]:ssc-sij replaces the fixed matrix
by a calculator called at every prepare. Running the analysis both ways and comparing
the posteriors tests the fixed-$S_{ij}$ approximation.

The comparison requires two conditions.

The normalization must be kept. For a Gaussian likelihood,
$$
-2\ln L = \left(N - \bar{N}\right)^\mathsf{T} C^{-1} \left(N - \bar{N}\right)
        + \ln \det C + n \ln 2\pi ,
$$
and the $\ln \det C$ term is constant only while $C$ is. When the covariance
varies with cosmology, dropping $\ln \det C$ removes the penalty on a larger
covariance, and the posterior shifts towards cosmologies with larger $C$. The
`use-norma` property of [[numcosmo-math|NcmDataGaussCov]] controls that term, and
[[numcosmo|NcDataClusterNCountsGauss]] aborts with `g_error()` when ssc-sij is set
and `use-norma` is `FALSE`.

The resampling covariance stays fixed. Only the fitting covariance follows the
cosmology; resampling uses the matrix given to
`nc_data_cluster_ncounts_gauss_set_resample_s_matrix()`, so the fixed and varying
analyses fit the same realization and differ only in the fitting covariance.
